items.title: Who are we?
items.text:
Cowthulu Games are a group of 4th Year Game Development students currently based in Dundalk. We are developing The Dancer for our final year collaborative project.

This Wiki contains:

  • Information about us as a Game Development Studio
  • Information about our game
  • Guides for the team to work on the project
  • Notes and Research gathered while developing the project
  • Links to Team Resources

items.title: Our Game
items.text: The Dancer is a Top-Down Action RPG developed in Unreal Engine 5 about Irish Sign Language. It aims to introduce and teach players about ISL in a fun interactive environment. The game is designed to be suitable for gamers aged 7 to 25.

items.title: The Dancer - Legal and Ethical Considerations
items.text:
Seán Burke

30th October 2026
path: The Dancer - Legal and Ethical Considerations

items.title: About
items.text:
This document will go into detail about the legal and ethical issues that will arise during the development of The Dancer, and what we plan on doing handle each one.

Note: These are just the initial thoughts from our Concept phase that will likely need revisions in the future.
path: The Dancer - Legal and Ethical Considerations

items.title: Legal & Data Protection
items.text:
Due to our game being an educational experience, we aim to track player data and storing it to improve the development of our game.

Things we will be tracking include:

  • Age Range: 7-13, 13-18 etc.
  • Tutorial Completion Duration: How long it took them to complete the intro area
  • Sign Success Rate: How many times the failed the sign system before getting the correct one
  • Level Completion Duration: How long it took them to complete the full level
  • Interactable Interact %: How many of the interactable environment objects they intracted with
  • Guide Interactions: How many of the menu guides did they look through
path: The Dancer - Legal and Ethical Considerations

items.title: User Consent
items.text:
• We don't track anything without the users explicit consent.
  • Consent forms will be clearly presented to the user on launch.
  • No hidden data collection, a full easy to read and understand modal.
path: The Dancer - Legal and Ethical Considerations

items.title: Confidentiality
items.text:
• User data is never shared to third-parties.
  • Everything is kept within the studio and stored securely.
  • Data will not be given to LLM's
  • Data is used only to improve the educational experience.
path: The Dancer - Legal and Ethical Considerations

items.title: GDPR Compliant
items.text:
• Our practices of tracking and storing data are GDPR Compliant.
  • Parental / Guardian Consent for users under 16.
  • Externally Accessible information on all privacy information.
  • Collection is anonymous
  • Data will be deleted at an institution approved date.
path: The Dancer - Legal and Ethical Considerations

items.title: Ethics & Responsible Practice
items.text: While we have good intentions developing a game about Irish Sign Language, it is crucial that we treat the subject with the respect and sensitivity that it deserves.
path: The Dancer - Legal and Ethical Considerations

items.title: Sensitivity
items.text: While we are building a game around ISL, we have to be certain to not just gamify any disability that requires someone to learn how to speak ISL. Our game is meant to introduce and educate users, not use ISL as a gimmick to make something unique.
path: The Dancer - Legal and Ethical Considerations

items.title: Representation
items.text: We will ensure that were are representing Irish Sign Language in a positive light. The Dancer won't feature any mature content such as gore, innapropriate language and excessive violence.
path: The Dancer - Legal and Ethical Considerations

items.title: ISL Informed
items.text: Everyone on the team will be properly educated on everything they need to know about Irish Sign Language and any other related topics represented by our game.
path: The Dancer - Legal and Ethical Considerations

items.title: The Dancer - Technical Design
items.text:
Seán Burke

30th October 2026

items.title: About
items.text:
This document will discuss the early technical design and concepts for the dancer ahead of our Concept Presentation.

Note: This is just the summary of the initial research and findings ahead of the initial Unreal Engine 5 Implementation.

items.title: Project Details
items.text: Title: The Dancer Engine: Unreal Engine 5.8 Version Control: Diversion Genre: Action RPG Perspective: Top Down Art Style: 3D Stylised Fantasy Unreal Plugins: FlatNodes, Diversion, GAS, Common UI

items.title: Unreal Plugins
items.text:
What specialised plugins will we have enabled in our Unreal Engine 5 project.

Plugin What does it do? Flat Nodes Simplified Blueprint node styling that makes graphs easier to read and understand Diversion Direct engine integration for Diversion Version Control Gameplay Ability System For advanced gameplay down the line provides Attributes, Tags, Gameplay Effects and Gameplay Abilities Common UI Advanced Frontend Plugin driven by abstract user actions and UI Navigation through UI Layers and Activatable Widget Stacks

items.title: The User Interface
items.text:
The User Interface will play a crucial role in our game's educational aspect. To be an effective experience, especially for a younger audience, we need to make sure players can get everything they need in-game without having to spend ages in menus, reading material before-hand, or constantly tabbing out to read material externally. Everything MUST be provided through the flow of the game.

Developing our UI with Common UI gives us three major advantages: 1. Built in Controller Navigation 2. Abstract UI Actions ie. Confirm, Back etc. will in theory allow us to navigate the UI how we need. 3. Clear seperation of layers with Stack Navigation will allow us to cleanly navigate deep menus such as a full menu wiki on ISL.

items.title: The Gesture Detection & Motion Controls
items.text:
This was the most dissapointing aspect so far but motion detection through specialised devices and software will likely not be possible for now. We did have luck however with motion controls and came up with a promising concept for handling fingure detection. The gyroscoped controllers such as the Playstation DualShock and Switch Joycons would be perfect candidates for detection user hand motions, we can then come up with an intuative user input for each of the fingers.

After doing some research we believed the Leap Motion Controller 2 would be the perfect device. It had software, a UE5 Plugin and great functionality for what we wanted, but the product was discontinued over 2 years ago and moved to end of life. This was after Leapmotion were merged with another company who went on to can their XR division.

This puts us in a tough situation where: 1. Buying a controller is incredibly difficult and expensive. 2. We would be making a product build around dead tech, that if someone was interested in, they couldn't actually use because they also can't buy the device.

After doing some digging I discovered that consumer standalone hand detection never took off as a product, instead XR and VR devices began integrating hand detection as a core feature and developers moved away from consumer products to industry manufacturing.

Another option for WebCam detection would be integrating Google Media Pipe into UE5, but that would be a large amount of work. There have not been any serious attempts at this since UE4 over 5 years ago so it would a large undertaking. It isn't simple hand detection, it is a machine learning library you have to train yourself.

Due to all this, our focus in pre-production will be aimed at a motion-control gamepad system with custom built finger position toggling.

items.title: Production Plan
items.text:
Some Must Have, Should Have, Could Have and Won't Have features.

Priority Feature Must Have Educational ISL Elements Should Have Generic Gesture Controls Could Have 3D ISL Representation Won’t Have VR / XR Gameplay

items.title: Anticipated Challenges
items.text: Some of the issues we will need to tackle as the project progresses.

items.title: Tactile Controls
items.text: Ensuring that the user can correctly sign using the game controller and the game can pick it up effectively will be the biggest technical challenge.

items.title: Educational Effectiveness
items.text: Will players come out of the experience feeling like they learned anything meaningful about Irish Sign Language after playing? Will our systems be able to represent ISL well enough and teach enough information in-game?

items.title: ISL Representation In Game
items.text: Being able to effectively represent Irish Sign Language in game through UI, 3D and Animations will require custom motion-capture.

items.title: Commmon UI Setup Guide
items.text: Seán Burke 4th October 2026

items.title: Overview
items.text: Since Unreal Engine 5 has it's own framework, there are a couple of steps you need to get used to doing with a new project. These revolve around the game mode and it's parameters, namely the Player Controller class. This document will go over the initial steps in order.

items.title: UI Scene Setup
items.text:
1. Make a Menu Player Controller
  2. Create a Game Mode and Assign the new Player Controller
  3. Add a Cine Camera Actor to the scene
  4. Create your Primary Layout Widget Blueprint
  5. Create your Base Button Class
  6. Create Common Text Styles
  7. Create Common Button Styles

items.title: Menu Camera
items.text: Add a Cine Camera Actor to the scene and position it how you want The camera needs a Tag named Default so it can be found efficiently

items.title: Menu Player Controller
items.text:
Create a new C++ Class inheriting from Player Controller. Override the base On Possess function so you can fetch the Camera from the scene. This will fetch the Cine Cam Actor you place in the scene for your main menu perspective.

```cpp void AMenuPlayerController::OnPossess(APawn* APawn) { Super::OnPossess(APawn);

TArray<AActor*> FoundCameras;
UGameplayStatics::GetAllActorsOfClassWithTag(this, ACameraActor::StaticClass(), FName("Default"), FoundCameras);

if (!FoundCameras.IsEmpty())
{
    SetViewTarget(FoundCameras[0]);
}

} ```

items.title: Menu Game Mode
items.text: Assign the newly created player controller in the slot Ensure the pawn slot is set to default pawn for now

items.title: Common UI Overview
items.text: Seán Burke 3rd October 2026

items.title: What is Common UI?
items.text: It is a plugin for User Inferaces in UE5 Developed originally for Fortnite but has since been adopted for all of Epic's games and larger samples.

items.title: What problems does it solve?
items.text:
• Managing multiple layers of UI where only the top should receive input.
  • Handling Gamepad navigation and focus.
  • Supporting different input devices and controller layouts.
  • Displaying the correct button prompts for the current active platform
  • Managing Activation and Deactivation of Widgets
  • Cleanly Handling Navigation between menus

items.title: Activatable Widgets
items.text:
Provides an explict active / inactive state for a UI Screen or component.

Useful for - Main Menus - Settings - Inventory - Pause Menus - Confirmation Modals & Dialogs - Pop-Up Windows - Submenus

The Activatable Widget remains in the UI Hierarchy while being inactive. This allows Common UI to determine which UI Layer should currently receive input. The widgets don't need to be constructed and destroyed every time.

items.title: Activatable Widget Stacks
items.text:
Activatable Widget Stakcs provide a stack based way of managing screens with Push and Pop functionality.

These stacks work in different layers such as - Menu - Modal - HUD - Notificaations

items.title: Input Routing
items.text: Input Routing is what makes Common UI's navigation work. It routs through the hierarchy of activatable widgets based on the layer order.

items.title: Common Input
items.text:
Common UI uses a system for describing Abstract UI Actions - Accept - Back - Confirm - Cancel - Navigate - Custom Special Actions

All of these can be mapped to different physical inputs based on the platform and controller. For example an abstract back action can be represented by different physical buttons. Controller Data Assets work with this to also provide the correct button icons for each platform and controller.

items.title: Common Widgets & Styles
items.text: Common UI provides its own version of widgets like buttons text etc. These can all be styled with central style assets. This allows for centralised UI customisation without needing to touch every single element of a widget.

items.title: What advantages does it have?
items.text:
• Better support for complex menu hierarchies thanks to layers of widget stacks.
  • Improved Controller support.
  • Platform specific button prompts.
  • Shared styling.
  • Clean menu lifecycle.
  • Scales better for large frontends.
  • Seperation of UI Actions from Physical inputs with abstract actions.

items.title: What disadvantages does it have?
items.text:
• Additional complexity
  • More setup
  • Migrating a project to Common UI takes time
  • Not every widget should be an activateable widget ie. Static HUD Elements
  • Not suitable for World Space UI

items.title: Potential Gesture Controls
items.text: Seán Burke 27th October 2026

items.title: The Goal
items.text:
Find a wide variety of controllers that could bring Irish Sign Language to life through a Desktop Game. This can come in the form of motion controls, gesture recognition, haptic controls, gyroscoping etc.

I will: - Research Potential Controls - Get Purchase Cost in Ireland - Research Unreal Engine 5 Integration

items.title: Potential Controllers
items.text:
• Ultraleap Leap Motion Controller 2: USB Infared Hand Tracker
  • Webcame with Google Mediapipe: Track Hand Movements
  • Motion Capture Gloves
  • Wii Remote Plus + Nunchuk: Funny Gimmick but could be good
  • Modern Gyro Gamepads: Dualsense and Nintendo Switch
  • VR Controllers: Experimental but could capture hand motion

items.title: Findings Summary
items.text:
While I found a wide variety of options, the majority were more gimmicky than feasible, but most importantly did not have direct Unreal Engine 5 integration and software.

All the controller variations would requiring some custom layers made - almost definitely requiring AI assistance and a considerable time sink. This made them more gimmicky - would be funny to show off one day if we have time options over solid examples we could build a prototype off of.

Some of the specialised webcam and glove options were also way too expensive for what would be a mediocre integration anyways, this rule them out pretty early on.

The WebCam is cheapest and quickest integration but it is just manually integrating a software plugin into a game engine - which could be a cool technical challenge but not worth the effort for what I believe would be an underwhelming experience.

This is where the Leap Motion Controller 2 stands out in it's pricing, software and technology. It appears to have peaked in popularity 2-3 years ago when it released, and since faded into relative obscurity, but for our game I think it's a perfect match at a great price.

The company just got bought out and is being merged but that shouldn't effect buying their product.

items.title: Best Option - Leap Motion Controller 2
items.text:
The Leap Motion Controller 2 is the standout from all the options. Everyone seems to attach it to VR Headsets but can be used without. Offers the best out of the box integration.

It does seem to not be available in many places however, and is being sold for over double it's initial launch price.

Cost: 285 Euro

Notes: - Comes with specific gemini software. - Sold for $129 at launch 3 years ago. - Small and compact - better than a webcame - offers VR level hand tracking - Comes with a game for Unity & Unreal - VR Oriented However - Used by VTubers

Videos: - UE5 Car Demo - Ultraleap 2 Intro - Basic Tutorial - VTuber Guide

items.title: Important Notice
items.text: Turns out it was discontinued 2 years ago, moved to end of life and not available ANYWHERE. This has one major problem, if we were able to get our hands on one we could make it work, however we would be developing and showcasing a game running on dead tech. If someone actually loved the game and wanted to set it up somewhere, they wouldn't be able to because they won't have the controller.

items.title: Second Best Option - Google Media Pipe with a Webcam
items.text: If we really wanted gesture recognition to the next best option would be a webcam with media pipe. However the gap in viability is quite large. I would not reccommend it as it hasn't had a well built Unreal Engine plugin since Unreal Engine 4. Using Media Pipe would involve creating a UE5 Integration layer ourselves, as well as the Python Machine Learning application ourselves. I don't think this would be a good move for now, would like to spend time developing a game as opposed to developing a plugin for something out of our depth.

items.title: Conclusion
items.text: The main takeaway with this motion capture tech I have seen is that it peaked 5-6 years ago and seems to have died off with the progression made by VR and XR Headsets. Everything I come across has either been abandoned or fully discontinued, for this reason I think we will be best suited going down the route of gamepads with motion controls. Maybe we can revisit it in the future if there are any developments but for now its a no-go.

items.title: Character Select Example
items.text:
What do we want to do?

  1. Get a list of all characters unlocked
  2. Display them
  3. When selected display them on a screen

What happens?

  1. Data Screen Component fetches the unlocked heroes
  2. It fires of it's delegate when completed
  3. The view screen component is listening to this
  4. It will create the buttons and send the data so the icons can appear
  5. When someone clicks on one of the icons, the view screen broadcasts the action saying this is whats clicked heres the data
  6. The action screen component takes this and opens the character selected screen in response

The System is Data Driven as its designed to avoid boilerplate. No C++ or Blueprints needed.

The Character Inventory screen then has all of these, but it also has an entry screen component. This allows it to broadcast out that it's data has been changed so it is entry as data can be entered.

Why is this good?

  1. It simplifies the interactions between screens
  2. You don't need to know anything about the screens themselves
  3. You only need to know about the component you want to interact with
